title: Dissolution of a Partnership Firm
description: Class 12 Accountancy: dissolution of a partnership firm — meaning and modes, the Realisation Account, settlement of accounts and the order of payment of liabilities under Section 48.

topics.title: Dissolution: Meaning and Modes
topics.concept:
It is important to distinguish two terms. Dissolution of partnership is merely a change in the relationship among partners (on admission, retirement or death) — the firm continues. Dissolution of the firm means the business is closed down completely: assets are sold, liabilities paid, and the firm ceases to exist. This chapter deals with the latter.

Dissolution of partnershipDissolution of firm
Relationship changes; business continuesBusiness closes entirely
Books are not closedBooks are closed; firm ends
E.g. admission, retirement, deathE.g. court order, agreement, insolvency

A firm may be dissolved in several modes:

  • By agreement — all partners agree to dissolve.
  • Compulsory dissolution — when all but one partner become insolvent, or the business becomes unlawful.
  • On the happening of certain events — expiry of the term, completion of the venture, or the death/insolvency of a partner (subject to agreement).
  • By notice — in a partnership at will, any partner may dissolve by notice.
  • By the court — e.g. a partner becomes of unsound mind, is guilty of misconduct, or the business runs only at a loss.

On dissolution of the firm, the central task is to realise (sell) the assets, pay off the liabilities, and distribute any surplus (or recover any deficiency) among the partners. This is done through a special account — the Realisation Account — studied next.

examples.problem: Example 1: Distinguish between dissolution of partnership and dissolution of firm.
examples.solution:
Continue vs close.

  • Dissolution of partnership: relationship changes, business continues.
  • Dissolution of firm: business closes entirely and the firm ends.
examples.answer: In dissolution of partnership the business continues (only the relationship changes); in dissolution of the firm the business is closed down completely.

examples.problem: Example 2: Name any two modes of dissolution of a firm.
examples.solution:
Pick from the list.

  • By agreement; by order of the court (also compulsory, by notice, on an event).
examples.answer: By agreement and by order of the court (others: compulsory, by notice, on a specified event).

examples.problem: Example 3: What is the central task on dissolution of a firm?
examples.solution:
Realise, pay, distribute.

  • Sell the assets, pay the liabilities, and distribute the surplus among partners.
examples.answer: To realise the assets, pay off the liabilities, and distribute the surplus (or recover the deficiency) among the partners.

recap:
• Dissolution of partnership: relationship changes, business continues. Dissolution of firm: business closes, firm ends.
  • Modes: by agreement, compulsory, on an event, by notice (partnership at will), by the court.
  • Core task: realise assets, pay liabilities, distribute the surplus — via the Realisation Account.

quiz.q: In dissolution of the FIRM, the business:
quiz.explanation: Dissolution of the firm means the business is wound up entirely.

quiz.q: In a partnership at will, a partner may dissolve the firm by:
quiz.explanation: A partnership at will can be dissolved by a partner's notice.

topics.title: The Realisation Account
topics.concept:
The Realisation Account is opened to record the sale of all assets and the payment of all liabilities, and to find the overall profit or loss on realisation. (Do not confuse it with the Revaluation Account used on admission/retirement — that only revalues; this one closes everything.)

The standard steps and entries:

  • Transfer assets (at book value, except cash/bank) to the debit: Realisation A/c Dr / To Sundry Assets.
  • Transfer outside liabilities to the credit: Sundry Liabilities A/c Dr / To Realisation A/c.
  • Assets sold for cash: Cash/Bank A/c Dr / To Realisation A/c (the actual amount realised).
  • Liabilities paid: Realisation A/c Dr / To Cash/Bank A/c.
  • Realisation expenses paid: Realisation A/c Dr / To Cash.
Dr — Realisation Account — Cr 
To Sundry Assets (book value)By Sundry Liabilities (book value)
To Cash (liabilities paid)By Cash (assets realised)
To Cash (realisation expenses)By partners (assets taken over)
To profit transferred to partners (PSR)or By loss transferred to partners (PSR)

The balancing figure is the profit or loss on realisation, transferred to all partners' capital accounts in their profit-sharing ratio. Key points: cash/bank is not transferred to Realisation (it is the medium of payment); accumulated reserves and the P&L balance are distributed directly to capitals (not through Realisation); and if a partner takes over an asset, his capital is debited and Realisation credited with the agreed value.

examples.problem: Example 1: What is the purpose of the Realisation Account?
examples.solution:
Close assets/liabilities.

  • To record the sale of assets and payment of liabilities, and find the profit/loss on realisation.
examples.answer: To record the realisation of assets and settlement of liabilities and to ascertain the profit or loss on realisation.

examples.problem: Example 2: Machinery (book Rs 60,000) is sold for Rs 70,000. What entry records the sale?
examples.solution:
Cash in, Realisation credited.

  • Cash/Bank A/c Dr 70,000; To Realisation A/c 70,000.
examples.answer: Cash/Bank A/c Dr 70,000; To Realisation A/c 70,000 (the surplus over book value becomes part of the realisation profit).

examples.problem: Example 3: In which ratio is the profit/loss on realisation shared?

recap:
• Realisation Account records sale of all assets & payment of all liabilities → profit/loss on realisation (shared in PSR).
  • Assets (except cash) transferred at book value to debit; liabilities to credit; cash from sales to credit; payments to debit.
  • Cash/bank is NOT transferred; reserves/P&L go directly to capitals; an asset taken over → partner's capital Dr, Realisation Cr.

quiz.q: The Realisation Account is opened to:
options: Record sale of assets and payment of liabilities
quiz.explanation: It records realisation of assets and settlement of liabilities.

quiz.q: Profit or loss on realisation is shared in the:
quiz.explanation: It is transferred to capitals in the profit-sharing ratio.

topics.title: Settlement of Accounts and Order of Payment
topics.concept:
After realisation, the cash available is applied in a fixed order of payment laid down by Section 48 of the Partnership Act. The sequence matters because cash may be insufficient:

  1. First, pay the firm's outside liabilities (creditors, bank loan, bills payable) and the expenses of realisation.
  2. Next, repay any partner's loan to the firm (a partner who lent money, separate from capital).
  3. Then, pay the partners' capital balances.
  4. Finally, any surplus is divided among the partners in their profit-sharing ratio.

The treatment of losses follows the same logic in reverse: a loss on realisation is borne by partners in their PSR. If, after everything, a partner's capital account shows a debit balance, he must bring in cash to clear it. If he is insolvent and cannot pay, his deficiency is borne by the solvent partners (under the Garner v. Murray rule, in their capital ratio, though the basic syllabus often shares it in the PSR — follow the question).

Other accounts used: the Cash/Bank Account records all receipts and payments and must finally balance to nil; the Partners' Capital Accounts receive the realisation profit/loss, reserves and the loan/capital settlements. When all three — Realisation, Cash and Capital accounts — close to nil, the firm is fully wound up. For example, with cash of Rs 2,00,000 and creditors Rs 80,000, a partner's loan Rs 30,000 and capitals Rs 90,000, the order is: pay creditors 80,000, then the loan 30,000, then capitals 90,000 — leaving nil. Mastering this order is the final piece of partnership accounting.

examples.problem: Example 1: Under Section 48, what is paid FIRST on dissolution?
examples.solution:
Outsiders first.

  • The firm's outside liabilities (creditors, loans) and realisation expenses.
examples.answer: The firm's outside liabilities (and realisation expenses) are paid first.

examples.problem: Example 2: Is a partner's loan paid before or after his capital?
examples.solution:
Loan before capital.

  • A partner's loan ranks before capital (but after outside liabilities).
examples.answer: Before his capital (a partner's loan is paid after outside creditors but before capital).

examples.problem: Example 3: A partner's capital account shows a debit balance after all adjustments. What must he do?
examples.solution:
Pay in.

  • He must bring in cash to clear the debit balance.
examples.answer: He must bring in cash to settle the debit balance (unless insolvent, when the solvent partners bear it).

recap:
• Order of payment (Sec 48): 1) outside liabilities & expenses, 2) partner's loan, 3) partners' capital, 4) surplus in PSR.
  • Loss on realisation borne in PSR; a partner with a debit capital balance brings in cash.
  • Realisation, Cash and Capital accounts all close to nil when the firm is wound up.

quiz.q: Under Section 48, the order of payment puts ____ first.
Any final surplus on dissolution is divided in the:
quiz.explanation: Surplus goes to partners in the profit-sharing ratio.

questions.q: Dissolution of the FIRM means the business is:
questions.explanation: The firm ceases to exist.

questions.q: Admission and retirement are examples of dissolution of:
questions.explanation: They change the relationship; the business continues.

questions.q: In a partnership at will, a firm may be dissolved by:
questions.explanation: A partner's notice dissolves a partnership at will.

questions.q: The account opened on dissolution of the firm is the:
questions.explanation: The Realisation Account records winding up.

questions.q: Which is NOT transferred to the Realisation Account?
questions.explanation: Cash/bank is the medium of payment, not transferred.

questions.q: Assets are transferred to the Realisation Account at:
questions.explanation: Assets go in at book value (except cash).

questions.q: Outside liabilities are transferred to the ____ of the Realisation Account.
questions.explanation: Liabilities are credited to Realisation.

questions.q: Machinery (book 50,000) sold for 60,000 is recorded by:
options: Cash A/c Dr 60,000; To Realisation A/c 60,000
questions.explanation: Actual cash realised is debited to cash, credited to Realisation.

questions.q: If a partner takes over an asset, his capital is ____ and Realisation credited.
questions.explanation: His capital is debited with the agreed value.

questions.q: Profit or loss on realisation is shared in the:
questions.explanation: It is shared in the PSR.

questions.q: Under Section 48, payment is made FIRST to:
questions.explanation: Outside liabilities and expenses come first.

questions.q: A partner's loan is paid:
options: After outside creditors but before capital
questions.explanation: Partner's loan ranks after creditors, before capital.

questions.q: Realisation expenses are recorded by debiting:
questions.explanation: Realisation A/c Dr; To Cash for expenses.

questions.q: Accumulated reserves on dissolution are transferred to:
questions.explanation: Reserves go directly to capitals, not through Realisation.

questions.q: When fully wound up, the Realisation, Cash and Capital accounts all close to:
questions.explanation: All accounts close to nil when the firm is wound up.

questions.q: Why is the Realisation Account fundamentally different from the Revaluation Account?
options: Realisation closes all assets/liabilities on dissolution; Revaluation only restates values during reconstitution
questions.explanation: Realisation winds the firm up; Revaluation merely adjusts book values while the firm continues.

questions.q: Sundry assets (book Rs 4,00,000) realise Rs 3,50,000; creditors Rs 1,00,000 are paid at Rs 95,000; expenses Rs 5,000. The realisation result is:
questions.explanation: Asset loss 50,000 − creditor gain 5,000 + expenses 5,000 = net loss 50,000.

questions.q: A creditor of Rs 40,000 accepts a machine (book Rs 35,000) in full settlement. The entry is:
options: No cash entry — the asset and liability cancel within Realisation
questions.explanation: When a creditor takes an asset in settlement, no cash moves; the items net off, affecting the realisation profit/loss only.

questions.q: Order of payment under Section 48: which sequence is correct?
options: Outside liabilities → partner's loan → partners' capital → surplus in PSR
questions.explanation: Creditors first, then partner loans, then capital, then surplus in PSR.

questions.q: A is to bear all realisation expenses of Rs 4,000 personally but the firm pays them. The entry is:
options: A's Capital A/c Dr 4,000; To Cash/Bank A/c 4,000
questions.explanation: Since A bears them personally, his capital (not Realisation) is charged when the firm pays.

questions.q: After all entries, B's capital shows a debit balance of Rs 12,000 and B is solvent. B must:
questions.explanation: A solvent partner with a debit capital balance pays the firm to clear it.

questions.q: Cash/Bank is NOT transferred to the Realisation Account because it is:
options: The medium used to make and receive payments
questions.explanation: Cash is the settling medium, so it stays in the Cash Account to record receipts and payments.

questions.q: An unrecorded asset of Rs 7,000 is sold for Rs 6,000 on dissolution. The realisation entry credits Realisation with:
questions.explanation: Unrecorded assets have no book value; only the cash realised (6,000) is credited to Realisation.

questions.q: A partner's loan to the firm is shown:
options: Separately and paid after creditors but before capital — not via Realisation
In the Realisation Account as a liability
questions.explanation: A partner's loan is settled through a separate loan account in the Section 48 order, not transferred to Realisation.

questions.q: If realisation yields a large profit, the partners' capital accounts will, other things equal, end with:
options: Larger credit balances payable to them
questions.explanation: Realisation profit is credited to capitals in the PSR, increasing the amounts ultimately paid out to partners.
